I smiled and let the sights settle quietly in my mind. The gulls, the masts, the singing men, all of it would stay with me for a long while.

So I went at once to a small room at the top of an old house, where my great-uncle kept his papers. The room was dim, and dust lay thick on the wooden shelves. In the corner sat a wide chest, and inside it lay a bundle of old maps, tied with faded string.

I spread them across the table, one by one. The paper was yellow and soft at the edges. Some were drawn by hand, with careful curls of ink and tiny painted ships.

I ran my finger over the southern seas. They stretched wide and wild, far past any harbor I had ever seen. Along the coasts of Patagonia the mapmakers had written short notes in faded letters. Some said only, here be strange waters.

What excited me most were the empty spaces. Across whole corners of the paper there were no shores at all, only blank sheets. Who could say what swam there? I pictured great shapes moving under the cold waves, slow and enormous, as the whale must be.

The more blank paper I found, the more my heart beat fast. Every empty space seemed to call out to me, like a door left open in the dark.

At last I rolled the maps up again and tied the string. I sat for a while with my hands resting on the bundle. My mind was full of wonder, and the whale was back in my thoughts once more.

I stood up and looked out the window at the gray street below. Somewhere out past the horizon, the sea was waiting, wide and unknown, and so was the great creature that lived in it.

I sat by the open window of my room and let the quiet settle over me. Far off, I could hear the waves breaking on the shore, slow and steady, like a heartbeat that never tired.

I remembered the evenings of my childhood. Back then, the sea seemed to call me from beyond the hills. I would stand at the edge of the water and wish I could sail past the last visible rock.

I did not fight the feeling. I decided it was a kind of friendship, the sort a man forms with the sea over many years. A friend does not always speak plainly, but he is always there.

I took a deep breath and let my thoughts drift. They turned, as I knew they would, toward the great whale. I pictured him rolling through distant waters, vast and silent, and I waited to see where my thoughts would lead me next.

The sea outside grew louder as the evening deepened. Its voice seemed to say that the way was open, and that I had only to follow it.

So I went down to the wharf one grey morning, my hands deep in my coat pockets. The air smelled of tar, salt, and wet wood. I wanted to learn more about the great whale before I signed anything.

Near a stack of barrels sat an old sailor. His face was weathered like driftwood, and he was mending a thick coil of rope with quick, patient fingers. I walked over and cleared my throat.

“Pardon me,” I said. “Have you ever seen a whale?”

He looked up, and then he laughed, a deep laugh that rolled out like a wave on the shore. “Seen one? Lad, I’ve seen a dozen. Once, off the coast in a fog so thick you could hardly see your own bowsprit, a great pale shape rose out of the water. It was as white as a snow hill, and it blew a fountain higher than our mainmast.”

His eyes twinkled as he talked. He told the tale with a grin, as if it were the best joke in the world. I listened closely, my heart beating faster with each word.

“Thank you, sir,” I said at last. “You have given me a great deal to think about.”

He nodded and went back to his rope, humming a sea tune under his breath. I stood there a moment longer, feeling the old itch for faraway things grow stronger inside me.

I walked on along the wharf, past the ships and the shouting dockhands. My steps were quick and eager. The gulls wheeled overhead, crying out over the harbour.

But my thoughts kept returning to the whale. I pictured that pale shape rising from the dark water, silent and enormous. I could not shake the picture from my mind, and I did not want to.

I sat down on my sea chest that evening and opened my notebook. The lamp swung gently above me, and the ship creaked around me like an old friend clearing its throat.

I decided to make a list. Sailors are fond of lists, and so, I confess, am I.

First, I wrote flying fish, skimming over the waves like silver darts. Then I wrote icebergs, tall and white and cold enough to make a man shiver just by thinking of them. Next came distant islands, green and strange, with names I had never heard spoken aloud.

I paused, pen in hand. Then I wrote the great whale at the very top of the page, and I underlined it twice.

As I looked at the list, my heart grew warm. Each sight seemed to rise up before me. I could almost see the flying fish leaping, the icebergs glowing blue, and the islands rising from the mist.

The list made me feel brave. It made me feel ready for whatever the sea might bring.

At last I closed the notebook with a soft snap. My thoughts drifted back to the great whale, and to the endless sea stretching out ahead of us, wide and wild and waiting.

After his prayers, he tidied his things one by one. He folded his heavy grego and laid it over the chair. He set his boots side by side, neat as soldiers on parade. Nothing he did was rough or careless.

I began to think there was more kindness in him than I had supposed. A man who takes such care with his belongings is not likely to be cruel to strangers. My fear loosened a little, though not all the way.

I asked whether the captain had ever spoken about it himself.

“Never,” the sailor said. “And I would not ask him, if I were you. He does not care for questions, least of all about his past. He will look at you the way he looks at the sea, and you will feel very small.”

Ahab did not move from his place. He kept his eyes on every line, every hook and every man. If a rope slipped, he would see it first.

The ship leaned, then slowly steadied. The sea grew darker, and the sky turned the colour of old pewter. Still the men pulled, and still the lines held fast.

At last the mates called out that the lines were fast. The work was done. Ahab nodded once, though no one saw it clearly in the dusk.

He turned and walked back to the quarterdeck. His wooden leg struck the boards, one slow step after another. He paced there in silence, his thoughts fixed on the white whale somewhere beyond the horizon.

Below him the crew took their rest. Above him the first stars came out, cold and bright, over the quiet ship.

“Belay that rowing, lads,” he called. “We will try a different trick.”

I am sure the sea holds lessons for anyone patient enough to look. A whale does not give up its secrets easily, and neither do the men who hunt it.
